Based on the second part of the fundamental theorem of calculus, $g$ is an antiderivative of $f$:

$g'=f$

This table summarizes the relationship between various properties of a function $f$ and its antiderivative $g$:

When the function $f$ is... | The antiderivative $g=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is...
:-: | :-:
Positive $+$ | Increasing $\nearrow$
Negative $-$ | Decreasing $\searrow$
Increasing $\nearrow$ | Concave up $\cup$
Decreasing $\searrow$ | Concave down $\cap$
Changes sign / crosses the $x$-axis | Extremum point
Extremum point | Inflection point

This is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ is decreasing:

$f$ is negative.

This is the graph of $f$.

![Function f is graphed. The x-axis is unnumbered. The graph consists of a line. The line starts on the negative y-axis, moves horizontally to the right, and ends in quadrant 4.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/a2e34c8bbf893782c8f076bc9451ea8aa9a71408)

Let $g(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.

**What is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ is decreasing?**

[[☃ radio 1]]

choices.clue: $f$ being constant doesn't necessarily mean $g$ is decreasing. If $f$ was constant and *positive*, $g$ would be increasing.
While it's true that the direction of $f$ affects the concavity of $g$, the concavity of $f$ doesn't affect the direction of $g$.
choices.content: $f$ is neither concave up nor down.
